input: the argument in favour of retaining the float at 7% is essentially based on where the delay risk actually sits within the remaining programme of work. Much of what remains is interface work: tie-ins to plant that stays in service, deliveries whose dates the upgrade project does not control, and weather exposure on the outdoor scope. A delay in any one of these areas would arrive at the critical path with no allowance of its own, and the float within the programme is effectively the only provision available to absorb it. The lower alternative treats the float as a contingency for the project's own tasks, and on that reading a smaller figure would suffice, since the task estimates already contain their own allowances for overrun. The steering group, however, does not accept that reading. Float held at 7% is intended to cover the gaps between tasks: the handover that waits for a permit, the delivery that slips beyond its window, the tie-in that cannot begin until a shutdown commences. None of these gaps sits within any task estimate, and none would be removed by estimating the tasks more carefully. The Costs section sets out the cost of the programme on this basis; the float is fundamentally a time allowance, and its cost effect runs through the overall duration of the programme rather than through any single line of the table. Reducing the figure to the lower alternative would not, in itself, remove the delays; it would instead transfer them onto the completion date that the steering group has reported, and until FID those reported dates remain the basis on which the upgrade project is judged, so that a float consumed by the first interface delay would leave the completion date exposed to the risks it was intended to absorb, a position which the steering group is not prepared to
